headline: Four people leave NASA's fake Mars after 378 days

sources.title: They spent more than a year inside a NASA hangar in Houston simulating life on Mars. Now, they're finally out (Houston Public Media)
NASA crew prepares to exit Mars simulation after nearly 380 days (ABC13 Houston)
Crew from NASA's simulated Mars mission emerges after 378 days in isolation (Reuters, via bdnews24.com)

chunks.text: On October 31, 2026, four people {{came out}} of a fake Mars base after 378 days. They never left Earth. They were [[volunteers]] who {{signed up}} for a NASA [[simulation]], a test that copies life on Mars. NASA is the U.S. space agency. The four {{moved in}} on October 19, 2025. Their [[habitat]], or living space, was made by a 3D printer. It sits inside a [[hangar]], a huge aircraft building, at NASA's center in Houston. It has 1,700 [[square feet]], about the size of a three-bedroom house.

verbs.why: Workers come out of the mine at five. The crowd comes out of the stadium after the game. Four people came out of a fake Mars base after 378 days.

chunks.text: The crew {{went without}} sunlight, shopping and family visits for more than a year. They {{made do with}} [[limited supplies]], as a real crew on Mars would have to. They grew [[crops]] in [[soil]] made to be like Mars soil. They also practiced fake [[spacewalks]]. They had to {{figure out}} how to cut their own hair and fix the [[plumbing]]. They {{worked out}} a lot, too. The crew's [[commander]] calls it "extreme camping."

chunks.text: The crew was {{cut off}} from [[the outside world]]. Email was their only way to reach family and friends. Every message took up to 44 minutes to arrive, just like one from Mars. The commander joked that the crew had trouble {{keeping up with}} the news. For two weeks, no messages {{got through}} at all. This copied a real [[blackout]] that could happen if the sun came between Earth and Mars.

verbs.wrong: To make someone feel very sick
verbs.why: Heavy snow often cuts off small mountain towns. Some new parents feel cut off from their friends. The crew was cut off from the outside world.

verbs.wrong: To write news for other people
verbs.why: My dad keeps up with the news on his phone. She reads a paper every day to keep up with world events. The commander joked that the crew had trouble keeping up with the news.
My calls never get through when the network is busy. Her emails get through even when the internet is slow. For two weeks, no messages got through at all.

chunks.text: Now the crew faces two weeks of [[follow-up tests]]. NASA wants to learn how people {{hold up}} in [[isolation]]. It hopes to send astronauts to Mars as early as the 2030s. Another crew did the same test in 2023 and 2024. The next [[year-long]] study could start as soon as August 2027. The crew's [[medical officer]] was {{looking forward to}} seeing her husband smile when the door opened.

mainIdea.s: Four volunteers spent 378 days in a fake Mars base on Earth and left it on October 31. NASA is using their year of isolation to learn how real astronauts might manage a trip to Mars.
mainIdea.why: The volunteers came out after 378 days cut off inside a building in Houston. NASA wants to learn how people hold up before it sends astronauts.

mainIdea.s: A long NASA test in Houston has proved that a small crew can live safely on Mars. Its scientists now say the planet is ready for people, and the first flight will leave in August 2027.
mainIdea.why: Close, but NASA has not reported any results yet, and follow-up tests are only starting. August 2027 is the earliest start for another study on Earth, not a flight.

mainIdea.s: A new robot from the space agency has landed on Mars and sent home its first photos of the ground. Engineers hope these pictures will help them choose a safe spot for a future base there.
mainIdea.why: No robot landed on Mars here. Four volunteers signed up for a test on Earth, and they came out of a fake Mars base in Houston.

tf.s: Four volunteers came out of a fake Mars base in Houston.
tf.why: They came out on October 31, 2026, after 378 days inside the building.

tf.s: NASA has no plans for another long study like this one.
tf.why: Another study could start as soon as August 2027, when a new crew would move in for a year.

tf.s: NASA wants to learn how people hold up in isolation.
tf.why: NASA hopes to send astronauts to Mars, so it needs to know how people hold up far from home.

lines.text: Did you hear about the four people who {{came out}} of that fake Mars base in Houston?
A fake Mars base? So they weren't in space?
No, they never left Earth. They {{signed up}} for a NASA test and {{moved in}} back in October 2025.
And they stayed there the whole time?
For 378 days. They {{went without}} sunlight, shopping and visits from family.
[[You couldn't pay me]] to do that. I'd get [[cabin fever]] in a week.
Same here. And it was four people in a space the size of a three-bedroom house.
It must be easy to [[drive each other crazy]] in there.
Maybe, but they stayed busy. They {{made do with}} limited supplies, {{worked out}} a lot, and had to {{figure out}} how to cut their own hair.
Could they at least call home?
Only by email, and every message took a long time. For two weeks, nothing {{got through}}.
So they were really {{cut off}}. They must feel [[out of touch]] now.
The commander joked that they had trouble {{keeping up with}} the news.
Why does NASA want to do this?
It wants to learn how people {{hold up}} far from home, because it hopes to send astronauts to Mars.
What did the crew want most after all that time?
The medical officer was {{looking forward to}} seeing her husband smile when the door opened.
That's sweet. Still, [[better them than me]].
